{{Distinguish|Michael Frame (politician)}}{{Short description|American mathematician (born 1951)}}
{{Multiple issues|{{Third-party|date=July 2021}}}}
'''Michael Frame''' is an American [[mathematician]] and retired [[Yale University]] professor.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Michael Frame {{!}} Faculty of Arts and Sciences|url=https://fas.yale.edu/book/faculty-retirement-tributes-2016/michael-frame|website=fas.yale.edu|access-date=2020-05-05}}</ref> He is a co-author, along with Amelia Urry, of ''Fractal Worlds: Grown, Built, and Imagined''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fractal Worlds {{!}} Yale University Press|url=https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300197877/fractal-worlds|website=yalebooks.yale.edu|access-date=2020-05-05}}</ref> At [[Yale University|Yale]], he was a colleague of [[Benoit Mandelbrot]] and helped Mandelbrot develop a curriculum within the mathematics department.<ref name=":0" />

== Early years and education ==
Michael Frame was born in 1951 and grew up in [[St. Albans, West Virginia|St. Albans]], [[West Virginia]].<ref name=":1">{{cite web|title=Small Things and Big Things – The New Journal|date=26 October 2011|url=http://www.thenewjournalatyale.com/2011/10/small-things-and-big-things/|language=en-US|access-date=2020-05-05}}</ref> After leaving his [[physics]] major because the lab requirement was "something in biophysics with killing frogs,"<ref name=":1" /> Frame, a vegetarian, received a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[mathematics]] at [[Union College]] as a [[First-generation college students in the United States|first-generation college student]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1978, he completed a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in [[mathematics]] at [[Tulane University]].

== Teaching career ==
Michael Frame came to work at [[Yale University]] at the invitation of his colleague [[Benoit Mandelbrot]]. At Yale, Frame called himself "the stupidest guy in the department...the dimmest bulb in the pack here," and focused on his teaching contributions.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Frame-Work of Fractals|url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2010/04/the-frame-work-of-fractals/|last=Yu|first=Sherwin|date=2010-04-24|website=Yale Scientific Magazine|language=en-US|access-date=2020-05-05}}</ref> He received the McCredie Prize for best use of technology in teaching at Yale College, the Dylan Hixon '88 Prize for teaching excellence in the natural sciences, and the Yale [[Phi Beta Kappa]] chapter's DeVane medal for undergraduate teaching.<ref name=":0" />

== Work with Mandelbrot ==
Benoit Mandelbrot includes a section on Michael Frame in his posthumously published autobiography ''The Fractalist: Memoir of a Scientific Maverick.''<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Mandelbrot, Benoit B.|title=The fractalist : memoir of a scientific maverick|date=14 January 2014|isbn=978-0-307-38991-6|edition=First Vintage books|location=New York|oclc=868856534}}</ref> In the section, called "Michael Frame, Friend and Colleague," he calls Frame an "indispensable" professor.<ref name=":2" />

In 1997, Mandelbrot and Frame held a meeting of teachers of [[Fractal|fractal geometry]].<ref name=":2" /> According to Mandelbrot, as far as he knew, this was the "first scientific meeting totally dedicated to the teaching of fractals.<ref name=":2" /> This eventually culminated in the 2002 publication of the book ''Fractals, Graphics, and Mathematics Education'', which was co-authored by Frame and Mandelbrot.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Fractals, graphics, and mathematics education|date=2002|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|others=Frame, Michael., Mandelbrot, Benoit B.|isbn=0-88385-169-5|location=[Washington, DC]|oclc=50032121}}</ref>
